description: The primary tissue discussed in the review, characterized as highly adaptable and responsive to mechanical loading. It serves as the biological system in which mechanotransduction, bone mass regulation, and bone loss are examined.

A physical loading scenario applied to bone that acts as the central mechanical stimulus in the paper. It is described as an important regulator of bone mass and a driver of adaptive skeletal responses.
The ongoing mechanical condition to which bone is continuously subjected. It represents the baseline mechanical environment influencing bone adaptation and maintenance.
A mechanical input necessary for skeletal development. In the context of the review, it functions as a stimulus that supports bone formation and adaptation.
The magnitude-dependent mechanical deformation experienced by bone that determines adaptive changes in mass, shape, and microarchitecture. It is a key parameter in mechanotransduction.
Normal mechanical strain levels in adult bone that help maintain bone mass by suppressing bone resorption. This represents a protective mechanical context.
A high mechanical strain condition that exceeds physiological levels and is associated with adverse skeletal effects, including bone loss.
A reduced mechanical loading condition in which the skeleton is not adequately used. It is described as inducing bone loss.
Long-lived bone cells comprising more than 90% of bone cellularity and embedded in the bone matrix. They are identified as the main cells translating mechanical strain into regulatory signals.
The structural environment in which osteocytes are embedded. It provides the physical context for osteocyte connectivity and mechanosensing.
The interconnected cellular network formed by osteocytes extending to the bone surface. It is important for transmitting mechanical information throughout bone tissue.
The anatomical boundary reached by the osteocyte network. It is part of the structural context for mechanotransduction signaling.
The process by which mechanical strain is converted into biological signals in bone. It underlies skeletal adaptation to loading and is the central mechanism reviewed in the article.
A skeletal endpoint reflecting the amount of bone tissue. It is regulated by mechanical loading and maintained by physiological strain.
A structural skeletal endpoint that changes in response to mechanical loading and strain magnitude.
The fine structural organization of bone that adapts to mechanical strain. It is one of the outcomes altered by loading conditions.
The process of bone breakdown that is reduced by physiological strain and contributes to maintenance of bone mass.
A detrimental skeletal endpoint induced by excessive strain or bone disuse and associated with bone loss-related diseases.
Bone-forming cells that receive regulatory signals from osteocytes during mechanotransduction and contribute to adaptive bone responses.
Bone-resorbing cells regulated by osteocyte-derived signals in response to mechanical strain.
The changing external conditions to which bone adapts through mechanotransduction-mediated signaling and remodeling.
The survival and functional persistence of osteocytes, highlighted as an important biological response in bone mechanotransduction.
The underlying molecular pathways and events that explain how mechanical signals are sensed and converted into biological responses in bone.
The therapeutic application implied by the review as a future direction enabled by understanding osteocyte function and mechanotransduction mechanisms.

A biomechanical loading scenario that serves as the initiating stimulus for skeletal adaptation and osteocyte mechanotransduction. In this context it represents the physical input that bone cells sense and convert into downstream remodeling responses.

The adaptive biological process by which bone tissue responds to mechanical loading to maintain structure and function. It is central to bone growth and homeostasis and is driven by mechanosensing pathways in osteocytes and other bone cells.

The developmental and physiological endpoint reflecting increased or maintained bone formation and structural development. The text identifies it as dependent on Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction and normal skeletal response to loading.
The maintenance of stable bone mass and remodeling balance. It is described as being supported by skeletal adaptation to mechanical loading and orchestrated through osteocyte-mediated signaling.
Bone cells postulated to act as the central mechanosensory hub in the skeleton. They detect mechanical loads and coordinate downstream bone remodeling and bone-forming responses.
The coupled process of bone resorption and formation that is orchestrated by osteocytes in response to mechanical cues. It is the functional output of mechanotransduction in bone tissue.

The intracellular and membrane-level mechanisms by which osteocytes sense mechanical loads and transmit signals. This broad process category includes mechanosensors and downstream effectors involved in mechanotransduction.
The biological process of converting mechanical stimuli into cellular signals in bone cells. It is the core mechanism discussed in the review and underlies skeletal responses to loading.
Ion channel proteins implicated in bone-cell mechanotransduction. They have long been considered candidate mediators of the skeletal response to mechanical loads.
A class of ion channels that respond to mechanical force. In the text, Piezo1 is identified as a mechanosensitive ion channel critical for skeletal mechanotransduction.
A mechanosensitive ion channel identified as critical for normal bone growth and essential for the skeletal response to mechanical loading. It functions as a key mechanosensor in bone cells.

The physiological response of the skeleton to applied mechanical forces, including signaling and remodeling changes that support bone adaptation. It is described as dependent on Piezo1 and mechanosensory pathways.
Downstream factors produced or regulated in response to osteocyte mechanosensing that promote bone formation. They represent effectors linking mechanical sensing to anabolic skeletal responses.
Molecular components that detect mechanical stimuli in bone cells. The review emphasizes identifying these sensors and their downstream effectors to understand and modulate skeletal responses.

Molecules acting downstream of mechanosensors to propagate mechanical signals into cellular responses. They are functionally important for translating mechanosensing into regenerative or remodeling outcomes.
Repair or rebuilding responses that can be modulated through mechanosensor pathways in bone cells. The text frames these responses as potential therapeutic targets.

entity_name: THERAPIES TO TREAT THE BONE LOSS RELATED TO DISUSE OR ADVANCED AGE
description: Therapeutic strategies intended to counter bone loss associated with disuse or aging. The review suggests that understanding mechanosensors and effectors may enable development of such interventions.

entity_name: BONE LOSS RELATED TO DISUSE OR ADVANCED AGE
description: A pathological reduction in bone mass associated with reduced mechanical use or aging. It is presented as a clinically relevant endpoint that future therapies may aim to prevent or treat.
A low-mechanical-use context in which bone loss occurs. It modifies skeletal loading conditions and is relevant to the development of therapeutic strategies.
An aging-related physiological context associated with bone loss and altered skeletal responsiveness. It is mentioned as a condition under which mechanotransduction-based therapies may be needed.

The tissue context in which mechanotransduction and Wnt-mediated mechanical signaling are discussed. It serves as the biological setting for studying how mechanical loading is converted into biochemical responses that affect skeletal integrity.
A mechanical stimulation scenario applied to bone that initiates mechanotransduction. It is the central physical input described as being converted into biochemical changes within living cells.

The process by which mechanical energy is converted into biochemical changes within living cells. In this text, it is the overarching biological mechanism underlying bone's response to mechanical loading.

The mechanotransduction process occurring in bone cells, involving signaling pathways that translate mechanical cues into cellular responses. It is facilitated by Wnt signaling and related modulators.
A prominent cell biological signaling pathway involved in bone cell mechanotransduction. It mediates mechanical signaling and is influenced by multiple regulators described in the abstract.
A Wnt co-receptor identified as a crucial protein for mechanical signaling in bone. It is a key molecular target in the mechanotransduction pathway and is regulated by several modifiers.
A regulator of Lrp5 activity that plays an important role in mediating signaling efficiency through Lrp5. Its mechanical regulation is highlighted as part of bone mechanotransduction.
A modifier of Lrp5 activity involved in mediating signaling efficiency through Lrp5. It is part of the regulatory network controlling Wnt signaling in bone.
A co-receptor that modulates signaling efficiency through Lrp5 in the Wnt pathway. It functions as a regulatory component in bone mechanical signaling.
A family of molecular regulators implicated in the mechanical regulation of sclerostin. These members influence Wnt-related signaling responses to mechanical cues.

Mechanoresponsive factors that influence Wnt signaling and help organize receptor complexes involved in liberating Lrp5. They contribute to regulation of the pathway in response to mechanical stimulation.
A receptor-associated complex organized by R-spondins in the Wnt signaling context. It is part of the molecular machinery that affects Lrp5 availability and signaling.
A receptor complex organized by R-spondins that participates in liberating Lrp5. It is a key molecular assembly in Wnt pathway regulation.
A set of Wnt pathway-related molecular targets proposed as candidates for pharmacologic modulation. They are relevant for enhancing the beneficial effects of mechanical stimulation on bone.
A mechanical stimulation intervention mentioned as an example of making mechanical loading more beneficial. It is discussed as a modifiable stimulus that may improve skeletal integrity.
A bone health endpoint reflecting the structural and functional quality of the skeleton. The text frames it as a target for improvement through modulation of Wnt-based molecular pathways.
A clinically relevant adverse outcome representing the likelihood of bone fracture. The abstract identifies it as a key endpoint that may be reduced by improving mechanical stimulation responses.

Bone-resident cells studied as the exposed biological subject in this paper. They are the primary population in which mechanical loading-induced plasma membrane disruptions, mechanotransduction, and survival responses were examined.

A physiological mechanical stress exposure scenario applied to osteocytes both in vitro and in vivo. It includes fluid flow loading and treadmill exercise, and is the initiating stimulus for plasma membrane disruption and downstream mechanosensation events.
An in vitro mechanical loading scenario in which osteocytes are exposed to fluid flow. It is used to model physiological loading and to study how loading rate affects plasma membrane disruption.

An in vivo physiological loading scenario in which treadmill exercise is used to mechanically load osteocytes. It serves as the organism-level exposure condition for assessing membrane disruption in different skeletal locations.

Transient disruptions of the cell plasma membrane that occur during mechanical loading. In this study, PMD are the central mechanosensory event linking loading to molecular flux, mechanotransduction, and altered osteocyte survival.
Movement of molecules across disrupted cell membranes following PMD. This process is proposed to promote tissue adaptation and to contribute to mechanosensation in osteocytes.
The biological process by which osteocytes detect mechanical loading. The paper investigates PMD as a novel mechanosensation pathway in bone.
The downstream signaling process converting mechanical loading into cellular responses in osteocytes. In this study, it is initiated by PMD and includes calcium signaling and c-fos expression.
A signaling process activated downstream of PMD in osteocytes. It is part of the mechanotransduction response to mechanical loading.
Induction of c-fos expression as a downstream transcriptional response to PMD and mechanotransduction. It serves as a molecular readout of loading-induced signaling in osteocytes.
The viability or persistence of osteocytes after mechanical loading and PMD. The study indicates that altering PMD repair rates can change this endpoint.

The rate at which plasma membrane disruptions are repaired after loading-induced damage. This process is pharmacologically modifiable and influences downstream mechanotransduction and osteocyte survival.
A pharmacologic intervention context used to enhance or inhibit PMD repair rates. Although no specific compound is named, the text indicates drug-based modulation of membrane repair.
A skeletal anatomical setting characterized by weight-bearing loading, specifically the tibia. PMD increased in this location during treadmill exercise.
A skeletal anatomical setting with minimal weight-bearing load, specifically the skull. The loading-associated increase in PMD was not observed here.

entity_name: RAPID AS COMPARED TO GRADUAL APPLICATION OF LOADING
description: A loading-rate scenario contrasting rapid versus gradual application of mechanical load in fluid flow studies. Rapid loading preferentially promoted PMD formation.
The level of mechanical stress used as a proportionality context for PMD occurrence. It functions as a derived exposure-response descriptor in the study.

Bone cells discussed as the focal cellular population in the review. They are emphasized for their regional variation and their functional role in the craniomaxillofacial skeleton, where signaling changes affect bone structure and cell-network integrity.

The anatomical region of interest in which osteocyte function and Wnt/β-catenin signaling are discussed. It is the specific skeletal setting where altered signaling is linked to changes in bone mass, mineralization, micropetrosis, and osteonecrosis.

A signaling pathway highlighted as a key biological process in osteocytes. Elevated activity in the CMF skeleton is associated with altered bone mass, mineralization defects, micropetrosis, and osteonecrosis.
A skeletal outcome reflecting the amount of bone tissue. In the CMF skeleton, elevated Wnt/β-catenin signaling is described as affecting bone mass.
A structural bone outcome referring to bone size or amount of skeletal tissue. The review states that elevated Wnt/β-catenin signaling affects bone volume in the CMF skeleton.

entity_name: MINERALIZATION OF THE CANALICULAR NETWORK AND OSTEOCYTE LACUNAE
description: A bone mineralization process involving the canalicular network and osteocyte lacunae. It is reported to be affected by elevated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the CMF skeleton.
A localized osteocyte-associated structural network within bone. It is part of the mineralization process affected by elevated Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
Microscopic bone spaces that house osteocytes. Their mineralization is described as being altered by elevated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the CMF skeleton.
A pathological bone outcome characterized by abnormal mineralization. The text states that aberrant elevation in Wnt/β-catenin signaling can produce micropetrosis in CMF bone.
A disease-relevant bone outcome involving necrosis of craniomaxillofacial bone tissue. It is linked in the text to aberrant elevation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.

entity_name: SIGNALING NETWORK THAT CONNECTS OSTEOCYTES TO ONE ANOTHER, AND TO OSTEOBLASTS ON THE BONE SURFACE
description: The intercellular signaling network described as linking osteocytes with each other and with osteoblasts on the bone surface. Disruption of this network is proposed as a mechanism underlying micropetrosis and osteonecrosis.
Bone-forming cells located on the bone surface. They are mentioned as communication partners in the osteocyte signaling network affected by aberrant Wnt/β-catenin activity.

A biomechanical loading scenario that serves as the primary functional determinant of bone mass and architecture in the text. It represents the stimulus that induces adaptive skeletal responses, including changes in osteocyte signaling and bone remodeling.
The skeletal tissue/population context under study, specifically the tissue whose mass, architecture, and adaptive response are altered by mechanical loading and disuse.
Bone-resident cells that translate mechanical signals into remodeling responses. They are central to sensing loading-related stimuli and regulating sclerostin expression.
A signaling pathway involved in regulating bone's adaptive response to loading. Its components, including Sost/sclerostin, are implicated in osteogenic and anti-osteogenic control.
An anti-osteogenic canonical Wnt inhibitor whose expression is down-regulated by loading and increased during disuse. It is a key molecular regulator of bone adaptation and bone loss.
Mechanical strain generated by loading that influences osteocyte signaling and sclerostin expression. Increased strain is associated with reduced sclerostin production.
A reduced mechanical loading scenario characterized by decreased strain, increased sclerostin production, and bone loss.
A skeletal endpoint associated with disuse and increased sclerostin production. It reflects deterioration of bone mass under reduced mechanical stimulation.
A mouse experimental population genetically or functionally unable to reduce sclerostin expression in response to loading. These mice fail to gain bone with loading.
A mouse model lacking Sost, used to assess the role of sclerostin in skeletal adaptation. These mice show an enhanced osteogenic response to loading.
The bone-forming adaptive process triggered by mechanical loading. It is modulated by sclerostin and is enhanced in Sost knockout mice.
A signaling cascade proposed to participate in osteocyte sensing and transduction of loading-related stimuli into changes in sclerostin expression.
A signaling cascade implicated as part of the mechanotransduction network regulating sclerostin expression in response to loading.
A signaling cascade potentially involved in translating mechanical environment changes into altered sclerostin production.
A calcium and nitric oxide-related signaling cascade implicated in osteocyte mechanotransduction and regulation of sclerostin expression.
An insulin-like growth factor signaling cascade suggested to be involved in loading-related regulation of sclerostin expression.
Therapeutic antibodies targeting sclerostin, mentioned as an intervention that may act within a context of enhanced osteogenic potential to prevent or reverse skeletal deterioration.
A disease endpoint characterized by age-related skeletal structural deterioration that may be prevented or reversed by therapies affecting sclerostin and loading responses.
A structural bone deterioration endpoint characteristic of disuse and age-related osteoporosis, discussed as a target for therapeutic reversal.

A continuous biological process in which bone tissue is renewed and maintained through coordinated activity of bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells. In this text, it is central to bone functionality, homeostasis, and turnover rate, and is regulated by mechanotransduction pathways.

The functional state of bone tissue, including its ability to maintain structural integrity and physiological performance. It is presented as dependent on bone remodeling and mechanotransduction-mediated regulation.

Bone-resident cell population that predominantly participates in bone and cartilage remodeling. They sense external mechanical signals and contribute to mechanotransduction-driven control of bone metabolism and turnover.

Bone-forming cell population involved in bone and cartilage remodeling. They respond to mechanical signals and participate in mechanotransduction pathways that regulate bone metabolism and tissue maintenance.

Bone-resorbing cell population involved in bone and cartilage remodeling. They are part of the mechanosensitive cellular network that responds to external mechanical signals and influences bone turnover.
Cartilage cell population that participates in bone and cartilage remodeling. They sense mechanical cues and are implicated in mechanotransduction pathways relevant to tissue health and disease.

Mechanical stimuli from the environment that act as the initiating input for mechanotransduction in bone and cartilage cells. These signals influence cellular responses that regulate metabolism, turnover, and tissue homeostasis.

The process by which cells sense and convert external mechanical signals into biochemical responses. In this review, it is described as the underlying mechanism controlling bone homeostasis, function, and remodeling.
The balanced physiological maintenance of bone tissue structure and function. It is regulated by mechanotransduction pathways and is essential for preserving bone health.
The set of biochemical and cellular processes governing bone formation, resorption, and turnover. It is controlled by mechanotransduction signaling in response to mechanical cues.
The rate at which bone tissue is renewed through coupled formation and resorption. It is a functional endpoint influenced by mechanotransduction and cellular responses to mechanical signals.

Cross-talking molecular signaling networks that mediate mechanotransduction and preserve bone and cartilage tissue health. They are implicated in both normal maintenance and disease development when altered.
The preserved healthy state of bone and cartilage tissues. It is maintained by signaling pathways involved in mechanotransduction and is compromised when these pathways are altered.

Disruptions or changes in mechanotransduction signaling in bone, attributed to genetic, hormonal, and biomechanical factors. These alterations are considered responsible for bone and cartilage disease pathogenesis.
Inherited or molecular determinants that modify bone mechanotransduction pathways. In the text, they are cited as contributors to pathway alteration and disease susceptibility.
Endocrine influences that modify bone mechanotransduction pathways. They are described as one of the factors responsible for altered mechanosignaling and disease pathogenesis.
Mechanical and structural influences that affect bone mechanotransduction pathways. They are identified as contributors to pathway alteration and subsequent disease development.

entity_name: PATHOGENESIS OF BONE AND CARTILAGE DISEASES
description: The disease-causing process leading to bone and cartilage disorders. It is linked in the text to alterations in mechanotransduction pathways and aberrant signaling responses.
Abnormal mechanotransduction signaling changes that produce disease-like effects. These aberrations are described as a mechanistic basis for bone disease development.
Pathological effects resembling disease phenotypes that arise from aberrant mechanotransduction. They serve as evidence that pathway disruption can drive harmful tissue outcomes.

Mechano-responsive molecular components and downstream cascades discussed as candidates involved in bone disease development. They are also considered potential prognostic, diagnostic, and therapeutic targets.
The emergence and progression of bone disease. In the abstract, it is associated with mechano-responsive signaling molecules and aberrant mechanotransduction pathways.
Biological indicators proposed for predicting disease course or outcome. The review notes that mechanotransduction-related molecules may serve this role in bone disease.
Biological indicators proposed for identifying or diagnosing disease. The reviewed signaling molecules are discussed as potential diagnostic markers for bone disease.
Molecular entities or pathways that may be targeted for treatment. The text suggests that mechano-responsive signaling molecules and cascades could be exploited therapeutically in bone disease.

Bone-resident mechanosensitive cells that are the central biological subject of the review. They are described as the main cells responsible for sensing mechanical load and mediating downstream responses such as mechanotransduction and bone formation.

Cell-adhesion structures involving integrins that facilitate mechanical signal transmission in osteocytes. They are functionally linked to mechanotransduction and normal osteocyte responses to mechanical stimuli.

The process by which osteocytes convert mechanical stimuli into biochemical responses. It is a key process in bone biology and is supported by integrin-mediated adhesion and integrin subunits β1 and β3.
A bone anabolic outcome triggered by mechanical loading. The review states that integrin-based adhesions play an important role in this response.
A core osteocyte function discussed in the review, mediated in part by integrins and relevant to maintaining normal cell behavior and mechanosensing.
Cellular signaling activity in osteocytes that is influenced by integrin function and contributes to mechanotransduction and disease-related changes.
An integrin subunit required for osteocyte mechanotransduction. Antagonism of this subunit in osteocytes impaired responses to fluid shear stress.
An integrin subunit required for osteocyte mechanotransduction. Like β1, its antagonism in osteocytes impaired responses to fluid shear stress.
A mechanical loading scenario applied to osteocytes that elicits mechanotransduction responses. The text notes that antagonism of β1 and β3 integrins impaired responses to this stimulus.
A disease state associated in the review with altered integrin expression and function in osteocytes.
A disease state associated with altered integrin expression and function in osteocytes, indicating dysregulated mechanobiology.
A disease state involving metastatic involvement of bone that is associated with altered integrin expression and function in osteocytes.
The level or pattern of integrin expression in osteocytes, reported as altered in disease states such as osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and bone metastases.
The functional activity of integrins in osteocytes, including roles in adhesion, signaling, and mechanotransduction. Dysregulation is noted in disease.
A general disease context in which faulty integrins and dysregulated osteocyte integrin biology may contribute to abnormal function and potential therapeutic opportunities.
Potential future interventions suggested by the review to target faulty integrin mechanisms in disease and improve osteocyte-related pathology.

A biomechanical loading scenario that acts as the central exposure in the text. It generates biomechanical signals affecting skeletal tissues, with moderate loading described as beneficial for maintaining bone mass and cartilage homeostasis, while excessive or inappropriate loading can contribute to injury and degeneration.

A dynamic skeletal process involving bone formation and resorption that is influenced by mechanical loading. In the text, it is linked to cartilage integrity and underlying bone responses, and is part of the coupled tissue adaptation system relevant to bone loss prevention.

The process of preserving cartilage structure and homeostasis under biomechanical conditions. It is described as being supported by moderate mechanical loading and functionally connected to bone remodeling and cartilage degeneration.

Mechanical cues or signal inputs generated by loading that influence tissue behavior. These signals mediate the effects of mechanical loading on bone remodeling and cartilage maintenance and are implicated in pathway crosstalk.
A skeletal outcome reflecting the amount of bone tissue present. The text states that moderate loading is required to maintain bone mass, making it a key endpoint of mechanical adaptation.
The balanced maintenance of cartilage tissue structure and function. It is presented as a loading-sensitive biological state that is preserved by moderate mechanical loading.
A deleterious skeletal outcome that can result from mechanical loading according to the text. It represents an adverse structural endpoint of excessive or harmful loading.
A harmful deterioration of cartilage tissue described as a deleterious effect of loading. It is also contrasted with cartilage maintenance and is a target outcome for preventive loading strategies.
Structural abnormalities in cartilage that are associated with increased risk from bone marrow lesions. They represent a pathological cartilage endpoint linked to altered bone-cartilage interactions.
Pathological lesions in bone marrow that are associated with increased risk of developing cartilage defects. They serve as an adverse skeletal condition connected to cartilage pathology.
The structural and functional integrity of articular cartilage. The text notes that changes in this integrity are linked to remodeling responses in the underlying bone.
The bone tissue beneath articular cartilage that responds to changes in cartilage integrity. It is the anatomical substrate whose remodeling responses are linked to cartilage status.

Interacting signaling pathways that mediate communication between bone and cartilage tissues. The text emphasizes this crosstalk as a key mechanism in the coupled response to mechanical loading, particularly involving the Wnt pathway.

A signaling pathway specifically highlighted as participating in crosstalk between bone and cartilage maintenance/remodeling mechanisms. It is functionally significant in the mechanobiological interplay described in the abstract.

The time- and space-dependent interaction between bone remodeling and cartilage degeneration. It is described as complex and important for understanding how mechanical loading affects skeletal tissues.

A proposed intervention approach using controlled mechanical loading to achieve beneficial skeletal effects. It is intended to prevent bone loss and cartilage degeneration by optimizing loading conditions.
A detrimental skeletal endpoint that the therapeutic loading strategy aims to prevent. It reflects loss of bone tissue or density and is relevant to osteoporosis-related outcomes.

A mechanobiology-related biological process describing how mechanical cues influence cellular and tissue behavior. In this review, it is presented as a novel approach to attenuate tissue degeneration and to understand adaptation and regeneration mechanisms.
The process by which mechanical signals are converted into biochemical and cellular responses. It is central to the paper's discussion of mechanotransduction, tissue adaptation, and regeneration.
A degenerative tissue outcome that the review identifies as a target for attenuation through mechanical biology and optimized loading signals.

Time-varying mechanical loading cues characterized by parameters such as intensity and frequency. These signals are discussed as the initiating exposure-like stimulus that can regulate adaptation and regeneration.

Mechanical loading conditions tuned by intensity and frequency to produce beneficial biological responses. The text presents these as a refined exposure scenario capable of regulating adaptation and regeneration.
A loading parameter used to characterize the magnitude of dynamic mechanical signals. It functions as a key descriptor of the mechanical stimulus in mechanotransduction studies.
A loading parameter describing how often mechanical signals are applied. It is highlighted as an important determinant of the biological response to mechanical loading.
A biological process in which cells or tissues adjust to mechanical stimuli. The review emphasizes adaptation as a major outcome of mechanotransduction and mechanical loading.
The process of tissue restoration and renewal following mechanical stimulation or injury. It is a central biological endpoint discussed throughout the abstract.

Signal transduction pathways that convert mechanical inputs into downstream cellular responses. They are described as important for explaining observed effects such as healing, formation, and differentiation.
A beneficial tissue outcome associated with mechanical signaling and mechanotransduction. It reflects preservation of tissue structure under mechanical stimulation.
An improved repair outcome linked to mechanical loading and mechanotransduction. It indicates enhanced recovery of tissue function or structure.
A tissue-building outcome, likely referring to new tissue formation, that is promoted by mechanical signals in the context of regeneration.
The process by which cells acquire specialized phenotypes. The abstract identifies it as one of the biological responses regulated by mechanical signals.
The publication venue highlighted as a platform for advanced research in mechanotransduction and its translation to diagnosis and therapeutics.
The underlying biological processes that drive disease development or progression. The review frames mechanobiology as relevant to understanding these mechanisms.
A therapeutic application context in which mechanobiology and mechanotransduction may be translated. In the abstract, it is discussed as an area of development for mechanobiology.
A clinical endpoint or application area where mechanobiology research may be translated. The abstract notes its relevance as part of the journal's platform for translational research.
Therapeutic applications or strategies informed by mechanobiology and mechanotransduction. The abstract presents them as a translational goal of the field.
Application of mechanical force to cells or tissues. It is the central stimulus discussed as driving mechanotransduction, tissue adaptation, repair, and regeneration.
Mechanosensitive ion channels implicated in mechanotransduction. They are cited as a molecular pathway associated with cellular responses to mechanical loading.
A signaling pathway mentioned as part of mechanotransduction-associated molecular pathways. It contributes to downstream responses to mechanical stimuli.
The immune response process, identified as one of the pathways or response domains influenced by mechanical loading and mechanotransduction.
A developmental biological process mentioned as being affected by mechanotransduction-related pathways and mechanical loading.
A combined biological process encompassing tissue adaptation and repair, highlighted as a major mechanotransduction-related response in regeneration.
The differentiation of stem cells into specialized lineages. The abstract identifies it as a mechanotransduction-associated response relevant to tissue regeneration.
The restoration and renewal of tissue structure and function. It is the overarching biological context of the review and the main process influenced by mechanotransduction.
A repair-related outcome that is promoted by mechanical signals and mechanotransduction. It is discussed as part of the beneficial effects of mechanical loading.

The biological tissue discussed as the central subject of the paper. Bone is described as a multiphase material with mechanical functions, including load-bearing, fracture resistance, and adaptation to mechanical stress through changes in size, shape, and mineralization.

A mechanical stress scenario applied to bone that increases bone mineral density and improves bone strength. In this context it functions as the stimulus driving adaptive bone remodeling rather than a radiation exposure.

The physical loading conditions that bone experiences and responds to by adapting its size, shape, and tissue distribution. These stresses are the environmental/mechanical context for bone mechanotransduction.

The biological process by which bone senses mechanical forces and converts them into cellular and tissue-level responses. It is described as poorly understood and central to directing osteogenesis to regions where strengthening is needed.
Bone formation process that is directed to regions of high mechanical stress to improve bone strength. It is a downstream adaptive response linked to mechanosensing and mechanotransduction.

A quantitative bone property reflecting mineral content and stiffness-related strength. The text notes that small increases in BMD caused by mechanical loading can substantially improve bone strength.
The mechanical performance endpoint of bone, reflecting resistance to deformation, fracture, and fatigue. It is the main outcome discussed and is improved by mineralization and mechanical loading.
A mechanical durability endpoint describing how long bone can withstand repeated loading before failure. The text states that mechanical loading can extend bone fatigue life dramatically.

A failure outcome that bone resists through its material composition and structural adaptation. Bone size, shape, mineralization, and collagen content are described as determinants of fracture resistance.
The tough collagen-based structural component of bone matrix. It contributes toughness and reduces brittleness, thereby improving resistance to fracture.
Rigid mineral components intermingled with the collagenous matrix in bone. They provide stiffness and are essential for sufficient mineralization and mechanical competence.
The process of depositing mineral content into bone tissue. Adequate mineralization is necessary to prevent plastic deformation under load and to support stiffness and strength.
Cell membrane channel proteins identified as an emerging pathway in bone mechanotransduction. They are implicated as molecular mediators of mechanical sensing and signaling.
A signaling process involving ATP that is emerging as part of the mechanotransduction pathways in bone. It likely contributes to transducing mechanical stimuli into cellular responses.
Intracellular signaling intermediates involved in transmitting mechanotransduction signals in bone. The text specifically mentions prostaglandins and nitric oxide as examples.
Lipid signaling molecules mentioned as second messengers in bone mechanotransduction. They likely mediate downstream responses to mechanical loading.
A gaseous signaling molecule cited as a second messenger in bone mechanotransduction. It is implicated in translating mechanical stress into biological responses.
Growth factor signaling molecules emerging as part of the mechanotransduction pathways in bone. They may contribute to osteogenic and adaptive remodeling responses.
A signaling pathway identified as an emerging component of bone mechanotransduction. It is relevant to osteogenesis and adaptive bone remodeling.
Potential therapeutic targets suggested by further investigation of bone mechanotransduction mechanisms. These targets are relevant to developing interventions for osteoporosis.

A bone disease mentioned as the clinical condition for which mechanotransduction-related molecular mechanisms might reveal drug targets. It represents the disease-relevant endpoint motivating translational research.

The most abundant bone cells discussed as the central mechanosensitive subject in the paper. They sense mechanical loading through appendices in bone canaliculi, support skeletal homeostasis, promote their own survival under stimulation, and regulate bone formation and remodeling via WNT signaling and sclerostin.

A mechanical stimulation scenario acting as the key external stimulus in the study. It is described as pivotal for skeletal homeostasis and as the trigger for osteocyte-mediated signaling responses that preserve bone structure and function.
A broader mechanical input that activates osteocyte responses. In the text, it contributes to osteocyte survival and downstream preservation of bone mechanical properties and bone hydration.
The physiological process of maintaining stable skeletal structure and function. It is presented as dependent on mechanical loading and osteocyte mechanotransduction.
Specialized osteocyte appendages extending through bone canaliculi that participate in sensing mechanical stimuli. They are part of the structural basis for osteocyte mechanotransduction.
The localized bone microenvironment through which osteocyte appendices extend. It provides the anatomical context for mechanosensing and mechanical signal transmission in bone.
The viability and persistence of osteocytes under mechanical stimulation. It is linked to preservation of bone mechanical properties and maintenance of skeletal integrity.
The functional mechanical characteristics of bone that are preserved by osteocyte survival and mechanical stimulation. This endpoint reflects bone strength and structural competence.
The maintenance of water content within bone tissue, described as important for preserving bone mechanical properties. It is supported by mechanical stimulation and osteocyte activity.
The differentiation of mesenchymal precursors into osteoblasts. In the text, osteocytes regulate this process in response to mechanical loading through WNT signaling pathways.
Precursor cells that can undergo osteoblastic differentiation. They are the target population whose fate is influenced by osteocyte-mediated WNT signaling under mechanical loading.

Cell signaling pathways that regulate cell fate and commitment. The paper identifies them as key mediators through which osteocytes control osteoblastic differentiation in response to mechanical loading.
A developmental decision process regulated by WNT signaling. It is functionally relevant because it determines whether precursor cells adopt osteoblastic lineage commitment.
A protein produced by osteocytes that modulates WNT signaling pathways. It is a central molecular mediator of osteocyte control over bone formation and remodeling.
The gene encoding sclerostin. Mutations in Sost are described as having dramatic skeletal effects, highlighting its importance in bone biology and mechanoregulation.
The process of generating new bone tissue. The text frames osteocytes as master regulators of this process through mechanical control and WNT/sclerostin signaling.
Site-specific remodeling of bone tissue. It is described as being regulated by osteocytes, indicating a role in adapting bone structure to mechanical demands.
Therapeutic agents designed to inhibit sclerostin activity. The text notes their development as a strategy to promote bone regeneration in orthopedics and dentistry.
The regenerative restoration of bone tissue. It is presented as a potential clinical benefit of sclerostin inhibition.
The clinical field or application setting in which bone regeneration strategies such as sclerostin inhibition are relevant.
The clinical and translational setting where bone regeneration approaches may be applied, especially in relation to skeletal and oral tissue repair.
